scams.name: Maui Rental Car 'Damage Claim' & OGG Airport Rental Scams
scams.description:
Post-return damage-claim scams are pervasive on Maui rentals, with Avis specifically flagged as a repeat offender, and overnight pickups at Kahului Airport (OGG) carry their own logistical traps. The pattern takes several forms. First, OGG-based operators (Avis, Budget, Hertz, Dollar, Thrifty, Payless, Fox) charge post-return "damage claims" of $1,500–$4,500 for scratches that already existed at pickup or for damage fabricated after the car comes back. Second, counter agents pressure renters to accept "Island Collision Coverage" at $35–$45 per day even though credit-card rental coverage is valid in Hawaii. Third, "return full" fuel-policy traps record a pickup level 0.1 gallon below what was actually documented. Fourth, a "sand damage" clause unique to Hawaii rentals adds a $200–$500 "beach sand vacuuming fee" if any sand is visible at return. Fifth, "budget" off-airport operators tack on a "remote island surcharge" of $30 or more per day.

For older travelers renting on Maui, the protective playbook is straightforward. At pickup, shoot a video walk-around narrating every scratch, the tire condition, any wheel damage, windshield chips, and interior stains, backed by timestamped smartphone photos of all four sides plus the roof and undercarriage. Photograph the odometer and fuel gauge at both pickup and return. For Hawaii trips, use Costco Travel (costcotravel.com) or AutoSlash (autoslash.com) for pre-negotiated rates with transparent pricing. Prefer Hertz, Enterprise, or Alamo at OGG over Fox, Payless, and Thrifty, which draw the highest complaint rates. Decline "Island Collision Coverage" if your credit card provides Hawaii rental coverage — Chase Sapphire Preferred and Reserve, Amex Platinum, and most Visa Signature cards do cover Hawaii. Vacuum any visible sand before return, since Maui "sand damage fees" are real and hard to dispute. Return with the exact fuel level documented at pickup. And dispute any post-return damage claim within 48 hours through your credit card, using your photo and video evidence.
scams.avoidance: Shoot a video walk-around and timestamped photos at pickup (all four sides plus roof and undercarriage). Use Costco Travel or AutoSlash for transparent pre-negotiated rates. Prefer Hertz, Enterprise, or Alamo, and avoid Fox, Payless, and Thrifty. Decline "Island Collision" if your credit card covers Hawaii rentals. Vacuum sand before return, and dispute damage claims within 48 hours through your credit card.
scams.location: Kahului Airport (OGG) rental car facility, Kihei rental lot partners, Lahaina/Kaanapali hotel-partnered rental operators, off-airport 'budget' rental lots
scams.tldr: Maui rental operators (Avis especially) charge $1,500–$4,500 post-return "damage claims" for pre-existing or fabricated damage, push $35–$45/day "Island Collision Coverage" you don't need, and add $200–$500 "sand damage" fees if any beach sand is visible at return.

scams.name: Maui Road to Hana Tour Bait-and-Switch & Insolvent Operator Risk
scams.description:
Travelers report Road-to-Hana tour operators going insolvent in 2025, and many warn others to avoid the route altogether or describe it as a xenophobic tourist trap. The Road to Hana is a scenic 64-mile highway with more than 600 curves and over 50 one-lane bridges; legitimate guided day tours run $150–$220 per person from Kahului through Valley Isle Excursions, Holo Holo Maui Tours, or Polynesian Adventure Tours. The scams take several forms. Recently insolvent tour operators take bookings and then fail to deliver. Third-party GetYourGuide and Viator listings cancel day-of with credit-only refunds. Hotel concierges sell a "VIP Hana package" at $400 or more per person for what is really a $200-equivalent tour. A "private Hana tour" runs $800 or more when a shared one is $180. A "Hana waterfall plus luau combo" at $350 turns out to be two separate bookings. And in resident-only areas along the Road to Hana, some locals charge unofficial "access fees" of $5–$20 at "viewpoints" that are actually posted as private property.

For older travelers doing the Road to Hana, the clean playbook is as follows. Book guided tours directly with verified operators: Valley Isle Excursions (valleyisleexcursions.com, $180–$220), Holo Holo Maui Tours (holoholomauitours.com, $185), or Polynesian Adventure Tours ($170–$200). Avoid third-party GetYourGuide and Viator listings for the Road to Hana, where cancellation risk is high. If you self-drive, start at 6–7 a.m. with a full tank, bring snacks and water, and turn around at Hana Town — the "backside" beyond Hana is where the xenophobic tourist-trap problems travelers describe tend to occur. If you pay a local for access to a "viewpoint," understand that it is not an official fee; some locals exploit tourists, so park only at designated National Park Service or state sites. Book two to three weeks ahead for peak seasons (December, March, and July). And the "Magic of Maui" Road to Hana app ($19.99) is the most widely recommended self-drive audio guide.
scams.avoidance: Book direct: Valley Isle Excursions ($180–$220), Holo Holo Maui Tours ($185), or Polynesian Adventure Tours ($170–$200). Avoid GetYourGuide and Viator for the Road to Hana. If self-driving, start at 6–7 a.m. with a full tank and turn around at Hana Town. Refuse "local access fees" at viewpoints and use only National Park Service or state parks. Book two to three weeks ahead for peak, and consider the "Magic of Maui" app ($19.99).
scams.location: Road to Hana tour operator booking sites, hotel-concierge Hana tour desks, third-party GetYourGuide/Viator Road-to-Hana listings, Lahaina/Kaanapali tour kiosks
scams.tldr: Some Road-to-Hana tour operators go insolvent after taking bookings, third-party GetYourGuide and Viator listings cancel day-of with credit-only refunds, and concierges mark up $200 tours to $400-plus. Legitimate guided day tours run $150–$220 per person.

scams.name: Maui Timeshare: Hyatt Vacation Club, Westin, Hawaiian Island Experiences
scams.description:
Maui's timeshare operators are among the most aggressive in the United States, and travelers widely report struggling to exit Hyatt Vacation Club, warn about Hawaiian Island Experiences Vacation Club, and point to ongoing class-action litigation against Hyatt Vacation Club. There are premium-property complaints as well, including a documented case at the Waldorf Astoria Maui. The patterns are consistent. "Free Maui luau tickets" or a "free Kaanapali snorkel cruise" are offered in exchange for a 90-minute presentation. That presentation runs three to six hours and pushes $20,000–$150,000 "fractional ownership" or "vacation club" purchases aimed at older retirees. Hyatt Vacation Club, Westin Maui Resort, Hawaiian Island Experiences, and Marriott Maui Ocean Club all run aggressive sales offices. "Maintenance fees" of $1,500–$4,500 a year rise 6–8% annually. The resale market for Maui timeshares is typically $0–$2,000 despite purchase prices above $20,000. And "exit" companies charge $8,000–$18,000 upfront to help victims cancel — many of which are scams themselves.

For older travelers in Maui, the defensive posture is clear. Never accept "free luau tickets," a "free snorkel cruise," or a "free resort upgrade" in exchange for a 90-minute presentation; the time cost and pressure tactics make it a net negative. If you do attend, bring a printed "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. Hawaii offers a seven-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts, so if you sign under pressure, cancel immediately by certified mail. For rescission help, contact the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (cca.hawaii.gov/ocp) rather than "exit" companies charging $8,000 or more. If you are part of the 2025 Hyatt Vacation Club class action, consult timeshare-owner forums for details. And avoid "Hawaiian Island Experiences" and similar "travel club" names that obscure a timeshare structure.
scams.avoidance: Refuse all "free gift" offers tied to 90-minute presentations. If you attend, bring an "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. Use Hawaii's seven-day right of rescission by certified mail immediately. Contact the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (cca.hawaii.gov/ocp). Avoid "exit" companies charging $8,000 or more, and use the state OCP instead.
scams.location: Kaanapali resort timeshare sales offices (Hyatt Regency Maui, Westin Maui, Marriott Maui Ocean Club), Wailea Resort presentations, Lahaina tourist-strip 'concierge' kiosks
scams.tldr: Maui timeshare operators (Hyatt Vacation Club, Westin, Hawaiian Island Experiences, Marriott Maui Ocean Club) lure retirees with "free" luau tickets or snorkel cruises into three-to-six-hour pitches for $20,000–$150,000 purchases that resell for $0–$2,000. "Exit" companies charging $8,000-plus are often scams too.

scams.name: Maui Luau Tour Package Overcharge & 'Free Luau' Hook
scams.description:
Legitimate Maui luaus run $125–$250 per person for a three-hour dinner-and-show experience through Old Lahaina Luau, Feast at Lele, Drums of the Pacific (at the Hyatt Regency Maui), or Royal Lahaina Luau. Around these established venues, several scams operate. Hotel concierges sell a "Maui VIP Luau package" at $350 or more per person for a luau that costs $180 booked direct. "Free luau tickets" are offered in exchange for a timeshare presentation (covered in a separate entry). Third-party "luau package" resellers on Groupon or Facebook charge $180 or more for what costs $125 direct. A "private luau beach dinner" runs $600 or more per person but is really a standard $200 luau with reserved seating. And a "Maui Cultural Experience" combo pairing a catamaran sail with a luau runs $500 or more per person when the separate bookings total $320–$400.

For older travelers wanting a Maui luau, the honest playbook is to book direct with established venues: Old Lahaina Luau (oldlahainaluau.com, $145 adult, widely recommended as the most authentic); Feast at Lele (feastatlele.com, $225, upscale); Drums of the Pacific at the Hyatt Regency Maui ($155); and Royal Lahaina Luau ($120–$135). For a Wailea-area luau, the Grand Wailea "Honua'ula Luau" ($175) is a legitimate hotel-partnered option. Avoid "free luau ticket" offers that require a timeshare presentation, which are a net negative. Avoid inflated third-party Groupon and Facebook luau listings. Book two to three weeks ahead for peak seasons (December, March, and June through August). Pay by credit card for chargeback leverage. And know that legitimate package alternatives are available if you prefer one.
scams.avoidance: Book direct: Old Lahaina Luau ($145), Feast at Lele ($225), or Drums of the Pacific ($155); Royal Lahaina Luau ($120–$135) for a budget option. Refuse "free luau ticket" timeshare hooks. Avoid Groupon and Facebook luau resellers. Book two to three weeks ahead, and pay by credit card.
scams.location: Kaanapali luau venues (Feast at Lele, Old Lahaina Luau, Drums of the Pacific), Wailea Resort luau strips, hotel-concierge luau booking desks, Lahaina tour-kiosk luau operators
scams.tldr: Legitimate Maui luaus run $125–$250 per person, but concierges sell "VIP" versions at $350-plus, Groupon and Facebook resellers mark up $125 luaus to $180-plus, and "private beach dinner" or "cultural experience" combos pad standard luaus with big markups.

scams.name: OGG Airport Long-Term Parking & Transportation Scams
scams.description:
Travelers report the realities of long-term parking at Maui's Kahului Airport (OGG), which sits 3 miles from Kahului town, 27 miles from Kaanapali, and 19 miles from Wailea. Legitimate options include on-airport OGG parking ($21/day economy, $22/day short-term, $25/day garage) and an off-airport alternative, Maui Airport Parking ($15/day with a free shuttle, at mauiairportparking.com). The scams take several forms. Off-airport operators advertise "$8/day" online and then disappear with the deposit. "Car rental shuttle" touts at OGG charge $25 per person to off-airport "discount" lots with no verifiable operator. Operators branded "Maui Cruiser" or "Maui Shuttle Service" quote $150 per person for a Kaanapali transfer when the legitimate Speedi Shuttle is $60 per person and the Maui Bus is $2. Uber and Lyft from OGG run $45–$80 to Kaanapali or Wailea depending on surge. And "helicopter tour plus airport transfer" packages at $800 or more bundle a $200 transfer into a $600 tour.

For older travelers flying into OGG, the clean playbook is as follows. For most visits, a rental car is the standard Maui approach — use Costco Travel or AutoSlash for pre-negotiated rates. If you rent, park at the on-airport rental facility directly, with no shuttle needed. For non-rental transfers, Speedi Shuttle (speedishuttle.com, $60 per person to Kaanapali or Wailea) is the verified default; Maui Bus Route 35 or 20 covers Kahului to Kaanapali at $2 (schedule-limited, with a 1.5-hour ride); and Uber or Lyft runs $45–$80 depending on surge. For long-term parking on return flights, book Maui Airport Parking ($15/day with a free shuttle) directly at mauiairportparking.com rather than through third-party aggregators. Refuse "car rental shuttle" touts at OGG charging $25 per person, and use only the free rental-company shuttles. And for helicopter tours, book direct (Blue Hawaiian Helicopters, Sunshine Helicopters) and skip "transfer plus helicopter" bundles marked up 30–50%.
scams.avoidance: For most visits, rent a car using Costco Travel or AutoSlash pre-negotiated rates. For non-rental travel, use Speedi Shuttle ($60/person to Kaanapali or Wailea) or Maui Bus Route 35 or 20 ($2). For long-term parking, book Maui Airport Parking ($15/day) directly at mauiairportparking.com. Refuse "car rental shuttle" touts and use only free rental-company shuttles. For helicopter tours, book direct (Blue Hawaiian, Sunshine) and skip bundles.
scams.location: Kahului Airport (OGG) ground transportation, OGG long-term parking lots, 'rental car shuttle' touts, Maui Bus routes
scams.tldr: At OGG, "$8/day" parking lots vanish with your deposit, "car rental shuttle" touts charge $25 per person to phantom lots, and branded shuttle operators quote $150 per person for transfers that legitimately cost $60 (Speedi Shuttle) or $2 (Maui Bus).

scams.name: Post-Lahaina Wildfire 'Ironside Claims' & Recovery-Exploitation Scam
scams.description:
Travelers report a specific post-wildfire claims scam, run by an operator calling itself "Ironside Claims," going door to door in North Kihei after the Lahaina fire. Since the August 8, 2023, Lahaina fire — Maui's deadliest disaster — the recovery through 2025 and 2026 has spawned scam ecosystems targeting both residents and visitors. "Ironside Claims" and similar operators go door to door claiming to represent insurance companies and demanding "claim processing fees" of $500–$2,000. Fake "Lahaina wildfire relief charity" donation requests circulate, while legitimate recovery funds include the Maui Strong Fund (Hawaii Community Foundation) and Maui United Way; verify any charity at charitynavigator.org. "Fire tour" operators charge $80 or more per person for drive-by tours of the destruction — a practice that exploits tragedy and is widely condemned locally. "Fire-damaged property" real-estate solicitations press owners to sell below market. And some inflated Maui lodging pricing is justified as a "post-fire premium" (some of this reflects legitimate market conditions, but verify). Travelers also track lagging recovery forecasts and the legitimate volunteer and donation channels.

For older travelers visiting Maui in 2025 and 2026, the protective playbook is as follows. Refuse any "insurance claims" or "recovery inspector" solicitations; insurance companies do not send door-to-door representatives demanding cash fees. Verify any "Lahaina wildfire relief charity" at charitynavigator.org before donating — legitimate funds include the Maui Strong Fund (mauistrongfund.hawaiicommunityfoundation.org), Maui United Way, and American Red Cross Maui Disaster Relief. Avoid "fire tour" operators, which exploit tragedy and are widely condemned; to help, donate to recovery funds and buy from affected local businesses in restored West Maui areas (the Wharf Cinema Center district is partially recovered). For accommodation, be aware that West Maui and Lahaina lodging supply is still constrained through 2026, so book six or more months ahead and compare against pre-fire historical pricing. Legitimate Maui tourism options include Haleakala National Park ($30 park entry), the Maui Ocean Center ($42), Iao Valley State Park ($10 parking), and the 'Ohe'o Gulch / Kipahulu district of Haleakala National Park. To report scams, contact the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (cca.hawaii.gov/ocp).
scams.avoidance: Refuse door-to-door "insurance claims"; real insurers don't send unannounced reps. Verify charities at charitynavigator.org, and donate to the Maui Strong Fund or Maui United Way. Avoid "fire tour" operators, which exploit tragedy. Book West Maui lodging six or more months ahead, and compare against pre-fire historical pricing. Report scams to the Hawaii Office of Consumer Protection (cca.hawaii.gov/ocp).
scams.location: Maui residential areas affected by August 2023 Lahaina wildfire, North Kihei / Lahaina post-fire recovery zones, insurance claim processing, charitable donation solicitations
scams.tldr: After the August 2023 Lahaina fire, operators like "Ironside Claims" go door to door posing as insurance reps and demanding $500–$2,000 cash "processing fees," alongside fake relief charities, $80-plus "fire tour" operators that exploit tragedy, and below-market property solicitations.
